title: Multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours
scopeHtml: Scope: tenant isolation models, noisy neighbour defences, per-tenant quotas, tenant sharding.

notes.title: What multi-tenancy means
notes.html:
A tenant is one customer organisation (a company, a workspace, a school) using your shared software; multi-tenancy means many tenants share the same running system while their data stays separate. SaaS products (Slack, Shopify, Salesforce, Notion) are multi-tenant.

The core tension: sharing makes it cheap (one deploy, high utilisation), separating makes it safe and fair (no data leaks, no one tenant slowing others). Every design choice slides along that line.

Things that must be per-tenant: data, authorisation boundary, quotas/limits, configuration/feature flags, billing/metering, encryption keys (for strict customers), and observability (per-tenant metrics).

Worked example. B2B app with 5,000 tenants: 4,900 small (under 100 users), 90 medium, 10 enterprise (over 10k users, 70% of load). Single-tenant stacks for all would be 5,000 deployments; fully shared gives 1 deployment but a whale can hurt everyone. Real designs mix models by tenant tier.

Industry examples. Slack (workspace = tenant, sharded by workspace id), Shopify (shop = tenant, "pods"), Salesforce (the original multi-tenant metadata-driven platform), Atlassian Cloud, Notion (shards Postgres by workspace id).

Decision gravity. Tenant isolation model is a major one-way door: you carry it in schema, auth, backups and pricing. Always carry tenant_id from day one, even if you start with one tenant.

Everyday analogy. An apartment building: shared foundation, plumbing and lift (cost saving), but each flat has its own lock and meter.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to ask who the tenants are (a few huge enterprises or millions of tiny users).
  • Treating multi-tenancy as only a data question; limits, billing and keys matter too.

notes.title: Isolation models
notes.html:
There are three classic ways to store tenant data, trading isolation against cost and operations.

  1. Shared tables (pool): one schema, every row has tenant_id. Cheapest, simplest ops, best utilisation; weakest isolation (one missing WHERE leaks data).
  2. Schema per tenant: one database, a schema per tenant. Moderate isolation; schema migrations run N times; catalog bloat beyond a few thousand schemas.
  3. Database per tenant (silo): strongest isolation, per-tenant backup/restore, residency, encryption keys; highest cost and ops (N databases, connection pools, migrations).

Plus dedicated stack per tenant (cell/single-tenant deployment) for whales or regulated customers.

Shared tables Schema per tenant DB per tenant
Isolation Logical (code/RLS) Medium Strong
Cost per tenant Lowest Low High
Tenants supported Millions Thousands Hundreds to few thousand
Per-tenant restore Hard Medium Easy
Noisy neighbour risk High High (same DB) Low
Migrations One N N 
-- Postgres row level security as a safety net for shared tables
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint);
-- per request: SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '42';

Worked example. 100k tenants averaging 20 MB: shared tables hold 2 TB in one logical DB (shardable by tenant_id). Database per tenant would mean 100k databases with 100k idle connection pools; impossible on one Postgres, so choose pooling for small tenants and silos for the top 20.

Industry examples. Salesforce and Slack lean on shared infrastructure with tenant ids; AWS SaaS Lens describes pool/bridge/silo; Citus sells sharding by tenant; many B2B apps offer "dedicated instance" for enterprise (Atlassian Data Center, Slack Enterprise Grid for large orgs).

Decision gravity. Moving from pool to silo for a tenant is possible but costly (data export, routing). Design a tenant directory (tenant to shard/DB mapping) so tenants can be moved without code changes.

Everyday analogy. Shared dormitory beds with name tags (pool), separate rooms in a hotel (schema), separate houses (database).

Common interview traps.

  • Missing tenant_id filter in one query leaking data; fix with RLS, an ORM tenant scope, and tests.
  • Composite indexes without tenant_id first, making lookups slow.
  • Picking DB-per-tenant for 1M tiny customers.

notes.title: Tenant context and data safety
notes.html:
Resolve the tenant once at the edge, carry it explicitly, and enforce it in as many layers as possible.

Mechanism: tenant derived from the subdomain (acme.app.com), a claim in the JWT (tenant_id), or an API key. The gateway validates it and puts it into request context (and trace baggage). The data layer reads it from context and always applies it (ORM global filter, RLS, or tenant-prefixed keys such as t42:cart:u7 in Redis, t42/ prefix in S3 with IAM policy). Never trust a tenant_id from the request body.

class TenantFilter : OncePerRequestFilter() {
    override fun doFilterInternal(req: HttpServletRequest, res: HttpServletResponse, chain: FilterChain) {
        val tenant = jwt(req).claim("tenant_id") ?: return res.sendError(401)
        TenantContext.set(tenant)           // thread-local / coroutine context
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res) } finally { TenantContext.clear() }
    }
}

Worked example. Background jobs often lose context: a Kafka message needs tenantId in its header; a scheduled report job iterates tenants explicitly. A test runs every endpoint as tenant A with tenant B's ids and expects 404 (not 403, to avoid revealing existence).

Industry examples. Hibernate multi-tenancy, Django-tenants, Rails acts_as_tenant, Postgres RLS used by Supabase; AWS IAM aws:PrincipalTag for per-tenant S3 prefixes.

Decision gravity. Cheap to build in at the start, extremely costly to retrofit across caches, queues, search indexes and file stores.

Everyday analogy. A wristband colour checked at every door of a festival, not just the main gate.

Common interview traps.

  • Cache keys without tenant id (Tenant B sees Tenant A's cached page).
  • Search index shared without a mandatory tenant_id filter.
  • Losing tenant context in async jobs.

notes.title: The noisy neighbour problem
notes.html:
A noisy neighbour is a tenant that uses so much of a shared resource that others slow down or fail. It is the main operational risk of sharing.

Where it shows up: CPU and threads, DB connections and slow queries, cache memory eviction, disk IOPS, network bandwidth, queue depth (one tenant's 5M-message backlog delays everyone), locks on shared rows, and rate limits on third-party APIs.

Symptoms: p99 latency rises for all tenants while one tenant's request rate or query cost spikes; connection pool exhaustion; Kafka consumer lag concentrated in one tenant's keys; one shard's CPU at 95% while the rest idle. Metrics to have: per-tenant request count, latency, errors, DB time, bytes stored and queue depth.

Worked example. Shared worker pool of 100 threads. Tenant A starts a bulk export that holds 95 threads for 10 minutes; tenants B to Z (each normally 1 thread) now wait. p99 for others goes from 80 ms to 12 s. Without per-tenant caps a single customer's script is an outage.

Industry examples. AWS calls it the classic cloud-sharing problem (EC2 "noisy neighbour" on shared CPUs/disks); Shopify flash sales isolated into pods; Slack's Enterprise Grid; Stripe's per-user rate limits and load shedding; Cassandra/DynamoDB hot partitions from a single tenant key.

Decision gravity. Detecting it is cheap (per-tenant metrics, add from day one). Fixing it later without isolation primitives (quotas, queues per tenant, shards) is hard and often means moving the offender to its own shard.

Everyday analogy. One flat's loud party in a thin-walled building, or one person filling the shared bath so the others get no water.

Common interview traps.

  • Only fixing capacity (adding servers) rather than isolating.
  • No per-tenant observability, so no one can find the culprit.

notes.title: Defences: quotas, fair sharing and bulkheads
notes.html:
Prevent one tenant from taking more than a fair share, and contain the damage if they do.

Toolbox:

  • Per-tenant rate limits and quotas: token buckets keyed by tenant (requests/s, bytes/day, storage GB, seats), return 429, and tier by plan (free 10 rps, pro 100, enterprise 1,000).
  • Concurrency limits per tenant for expensive operations (exports, reports: max 2 at a time).
  • Fair queuing: per-tenant queues serviced round robin or weighted (not one global FIFO); prevents a 5M backlog from starving others. Kafka: partition by tenant carefully or use separate topics for heavy tenants.
  • Bulkheads: separate thread pools/connection pools per workload or tier, so a flooded pool does not take down others.
  • Query governance: statement timeouts (statement_timeout=5s), max rows, cost limits, pagination enforced.
  • Resource isolation: Kubernetes requests/limits and namespaces per tier, cgroup CPU shares, priority classes; separate "bulk" vs "interactive" worker fleets.
  • Load shedding for lowest-priority tenant traffic first.
# Kubernetes quota per tenant namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: {name: tenant-acme, namespace: acme}
spec:
  hard: {requests.cpu: "8", requests.memory: 16Gi, limits.cpu: "16", pods: "50"}
ALTER ROLE tenant_app SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE tenant_reports SET statement_timeout = '10min';  -- separate role and pool for heavy work

Worked example. 100 workers, 500 tenants. Rule: each tenant may hold at most 10 workers, and reserved capacity of 20 workers is only for "interactive" lane. Bulk exports run in a separate lane with 30 workers. Result: Tenant A's export uses at most 10 workers and cannot touch the interactive lane; others' p99 stays at 80 ms.

Industry examples. Stripe's 4 limiter types (request rate, concurrent requests, fleet usage load shedder, worker utilisation shedder); AWS service quotas per account; Salesforce governor limits (per-transaction caps on queries and CPU, a famous multi-tenant design); GitHub Actions concurrency limits per plan.

Decision gravity. Quotas are reversible config but are product-visible (customers hit them), so publish them and give clear errors. Governor-style hard limits designed from the start save the platform; adding them after launch breaks existing customers.

Everyday analogy. A buffet with a plate limit per person and separate lines for takeaway orders, so one greedy guest cannot empty the trays.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global queue or thread pool for all tenants.
  • Limits that are only global (not per tenant).
  • Retrying clients that amplify the flood after a 429.

notes.title: Sharding by tenant and cells
notes.html:
Because tenants rarely interact, tenant_id is a near-perfect shard key: all of a tenant's data lives together, queries stay local, and cross-shard joins vanish. Isolation also becomes physical.

Mechanism: a tenant directory table maps tenant_id -> shard. The router looks it up (cached) and sends the request to that shard's DB/cluster. New tenants go to the least-loaded shard; whales get a dedicated shard; a tenant can be moved (copy, dual-write or replicate, cut over, delete). Cell-based architecture takes this further: the whole stack (app + DB + cache + queue) is replicated into independent cells, each serving a subset of tenants; a router sends traffic to the right cell. A failure or bad deploy only affects one cell (blast radius = 1/N).

CREATE TABLE tenant_directory (
  tenant_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  cell      TEXT NOT NULL,       -- 'cell-eu-3'
  tier      TEXT NOT NULL,       -- 'pool' | 'silo'
  moved_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);

Worked example. 20 cells, each sized for 5,000 tenants and 2,000 requests/s at 50% headroom. A bad deploy to cell 7 affects 5% of tenants and is rolled back by routing, not redeployed everywhere. Capacity planning: add a cell when average utilisation hits 60%.

Industry examples. Slack moved to a cell-based architecture after outages; AWS builds services as cells (Route 53, DynamoDB, "static stability"); Shopify "pods" each with its own MySQL; Notion sharded Postgres by workspace into 480 logical shards (confirm numbers); Figma and Discord shard by account/guild.

Decision gravity. Choose the tenant directory (an indirection) early: it is the key that makes later moves and resharding possible. Hash-mod-N routing is a trap, because adding a shard remaps everyone. Cells are a heavy but powerful one-way commitment.

Everyday analogy. A city with identical neighbourhoods each with their own power grid: an outage hits one neighbourhood, and a new neighbourhood is built when old ones fill.

Common interview traps.

  • hash(tenant_id) % N without a directory.
  • Cross-tenant features (global search, admin analytics) that break sharding: route them to a separate warehouse.
  • Forgetting a "mega-tenant" that outgrows one shard.

notes.title: Tenant-level features: config, keys, billing
notes.html:
Tenants differ: they want different settings, encryption, data location and bills. Build these as first-class capabilities.

  • Configuration and feature flags per tenant (stored in a tenants table, cached with a short TTL; flags like LaunchDarkly by tenant attribute). Custom fields via JSONB or an EAV/metadata layer (Salesforce style).
  • Customer-managed keys (BYOK/CMK): per-tenant data key wrapped by a KMS key the customer controls; revoking the key makes the data unreadable (crypto-shredding for offboarding).
  • Data residency: EU tenants pinned to EU cells; the directory enforces placement.
  • Metering and billing: emit usage events (tenant, metric, quantity, timestamp) to Kafka, aggregate hourly into a usage table, feed Stripe Billing; idempotency keys avoid double counting.
  • Customisation: SSO per tenant (SAML/OIDC configs), custom domains, webhooks with per-tenant signing secrets.
  • Offboarding: export, then delete all copies (DB, caches, search, backups, logs) with a verifiable ledger.
{ "tenant_id": 42, "metric": "api_calls", "qty": 1, "ts": "2026-11-09T10:00:00Z", "event_id": "e-9f2" }

Worked example. 10M usage events/hour (about 2,800/s). Aggregate into (tenant, metric, hour) rows: 5,000 tenants x 10 metrics x 24 = 1.2M rows/day, trivial. Duplicate delivery is harmless because event_id is deduplicated.

Industry examples. Salesforce custom objects, AWS KMS customer-managed keys, Slack Enterprise Key Management, Stripe usage-based billing, Twilio per-account metering, Auth0 per-tenant connections.

Decision gravity. Metering and per-tenant keys are painful to bolt on; billing disputes rely on accurate, replayable usage logs, so store raw events durably.

Everyday analogy. A utility company with a separate meter and bill per flat, and some flats asking for their own padlock.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring offboarding and deletion (compliance).
  • Metering in a lossy path (best-effort logs) when the number is money.
  • One-size-fits-all configuration that forces code forks per customer.

notes.title: Choosing a strategy by tenant tier
notes.html:
Mix models: pool the long tail, silo the whales, and use cells to scale both.

Rule of thumb:

  • Free/small tenants (the long tail): shared tables, strict per-tenant limits, RLS.
  • Medium: shared cells with per-tenant quotas and fair queues.
  • Enterprise/regulated: dedicated shard or database, optional dedicated stack, customer-managed keys, residency pinning.
  • Everything routed through a tenant directory so tenants can be promoted from pool to silo without code change.

Decision checklist for the interview: how many tenants, size skew (top 1% share of load), compliance needs (residency, keys), availability targets, migration needs, and cost per tenant versus price.

Worked example. Revenue per tenant: free $0, pro $50/month, enterprise $10k/month. Infrastructure cost per pooled tenant: $0.20/month, dedicated DB $300/month. Dedicated DB for a $50 customer loses money; for a $10k customer it is 3% of revenue, so silo only above a revenue threshold.

Industry examples. Slack (shared + Enterprise Grid), Atlassian (cloud multi-tenant + Data Center), Salesforce Hyperforce (regional cells), MongoDB Atlas (shared M0/M2 clusters vs dedicated).

Decision gravity. The hybrid is the long-term norm; designing the directory and tenant-aware code from day one makes promoting a tenant a one-week task rather than a re-architecture.

Everyday analogy. Airlines: economy seats shared by many, business class with more space, and charters for those who pay for a whole plane.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking one model for everyone.
  • Ignoring unit economics when proposing dedicated infrastructure.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Multi-tenancy = many customers share one system with separated data, limits, config, keys and billing; carry tenant_id everywhere from day one.
  • Isolation models: shared tables (cheapest, RLS as safety net), schema per tenant, database per tenant (strong, costly), dedicated stacks for whales.
  • Resolve tenant at the edge (subdomain, JWT claim), propagate in context, enforce in DB, cache keys, search, object storage and async jobs.
  • Noisy neighbour = one tenant starving shared resources; watch per-tenant latency, DB time, queue depth.
  • Defend with per-tenant rate limits and quotas, concurrency caps, fair queues, bulkheads, statement timeouts, K8s quotas and load shedding.
  • Shard by tenant through a tenant directory (not hash % N); cell architecture limits blast radius and enables moves.
  • Per-tenant features: config/flags, customer-managed keys, residency, usage metering, offboarding deletion.
  • Use a tiered hybrid: pool the long tail, silo large or regulated tenants, all routed via the directory.

questions.promptHtml: What is multi-tenancy, and why must tenant_id be there from day one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SaaS design starts here; the answer shows you know the isolation, cost and security stakes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Multi-tenancy means one running system serves many customers (tenants) whose data and performance must stay separate. Sharing infrastructure is cheap but creates risks: data leaks between tenants and one tenant hurting others. I carry a tenant_id through schema, auth, caches, queues, search and files from day one, because retrofitting it later across all those stores is very expensive. The isolation model is a one-way door: it ends up in schema, backups and pricing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: 5,000 tenants: 4,900 small (under 100 users), 90 medium, 10 enterprise (over 10k users, 70% of load). Single-tenant stacks for everyone means 5,000 deployments; fully shared means 1 deployment but a whale can hurt everyone. Real designs mix models by tier.

Request -> authenticate -> resolve tenant -> tenant context -> every query filtered by tenant

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding tenant_id only to the main tables, forgetting cache keys, queue messages and search indexes.
  • Trusting a tenant id sent by the client instead of deriving it from the auth token.
  • Treating isolation as only a security issue (it is also performance and cost).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the tenant id come from? -> The verified token or subdomain, never from a request body.
  2. What about background jobs? -> Carry tenantId in message headers; scheduled jobs iterate tenants explicitly.
  3. Can you change the model later? -> Costly; a tenant directory helps.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "add a tenant column". Senior: all stores, tiers, directory, noisy neighbours and billing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search index without tenant filters leaked one customer's document titles in autocomplete.

questions.promptHtml: Compare shared tables, schema per tenant, and database per tenant. When do you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests cost, operations and isolation trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Shared tables with a tenant_id column (pool) are cheapest and easiest to operate but have the weakest isolation. Schema per tenant is the middle path. Database per tenant (silo) gives the strongest isolation, per-tenant backup and restore, and noisy-neighbour protection, at a high cost. For 100k small tenants, I pool; for the top 20 whales and regulated customers I use silos, and a tenant directory lets me move a tenant between them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: 100k tenants averaging 20 MB is 2 TB in shared tables (shardable by tenant_id). Database per tenant means 100k databases and 100k idle connection pools: not feasible on one Postgres. Postgres row-level security can enforce the filter in the DB:

ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);
Model Isolation Cost Ops
Shared tables Low Lowest Easy
Schema per tenant Medium Medium Migrations x N
DB per tenant High High Heavy

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Schema per tenant at 50k tenants: migrations and catalog bloat.
  • Assuming RLS alone stops noisy neighbours (it does not).
  • No way to move tenants later.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you migrate pool to silo? -> Export, route via the directory, cut over, verify.
  2. Per-tenant restore? -> Easy in silo, hard in a pool.
  3. Connection counts? -> Pooled connections (PgBouncer); silo per tenant multiplies them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE names the three. Senior ties each to tenant tier, cost per tenant and the directory.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with schema per tenant hit slow migrations at 8k tenants and moved small tenants into a pool.

questions.contextHtml:
A support engineer reports seeing another customer's invoice. The code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@GetMapping("/invoices/{id}")
Invoice get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return invoiceRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(NotFound::new);   // no tenant check
}
private final Cache<String, Invoice> cache = ...;   // key = invoice id only
@GetMapping("/invoices/{id}")
fun get(@PathVariable id: String): Invoice =
    invoiceRepo.findById(id) ?: throw NotFound()   // no tenant check
private val cache: Cache<String, Invoice> = ...      // key = invoice id only

Invoice ids are sequential integers. A nightly report job also iterates all invoices with no tenant set.
questions.promptHtml: List the bugs and the systematic fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only adds a WHERE tenant_id to this one query.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was it only ids guessed, or cached cross-tenant? How many endpoints are similar? Any logs of cross-tenant reads?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a tenant filter to this endpoint, flush the cache, notify security.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) IDOR with sequential ids; (b) cache key missing tenant; (c) background job without context; (d) other endpoints with the same pattern.
  4. How I'd verify: an automated test calling every endpoint as tenant A with tenant B's ids; grep the repos for queries without a tenant predicate; check access logs.
  5. Root cause: tenant filtering is left to each developer instead of enforced centrally.
  6. Fix: tenant context from the token, repository layer or RLS adds the predicate automatically; cache key tenant:id; non-guessable ids (UUID); return 404 not 403 to avoid revealing existence; jobs iterate tenants explicitly and set context.
  7. Prevention: the cross-tenant test as a CI gate; lint rule banning raw queries without tenant; DB RLS as a backstop.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not rely on UUIDs as a security measure alone; RLS has per-request SET overhead but is worth it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Admin needing cross-tenant access? -> Separate audited path with explicit scope.
  • Search index? -> Filter by tenant in every query, or a per-tenant routing key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared Redis cache key invoice:1042 leaked data between tenants for a week before an auditor noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches one query.
  • Hire: tenant-scoped cache, IDOR and a central enforcement.
  • Strong hire: cross-tenant CI test, RLS backstop, job context handling.

questions.promptHtml: What is the noisy neighbour problem and how do you detect it before customers report it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core multi-tenant ops skill: detection and attribution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One tenant's heavy usage consumes shared resources (threads, CPU, DB connections, IOPS, cache) and degrades others. Example: a shared 100-thread worker pool where tenant A's export holds 95 threads for 10 minutes pushes everybody else's p99 from 80 ms to 12 s. Detection needs per-tenant metrics from day one: requests, latency, queue time, resource use, top-N tenants by consumption. Without them you see only aggregate degradation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Shared resources worth tracking per tenant: thread/worker slots, DB connections and query time, cache memory, queue depth, bandwidth, IOPS. Dashboards: top 10 tenants by CPU-seconds, DB time, and rate of 429s. The fix needs isolation primitives (quotas, lanes, shards); detection is the cheap part.

Pool of 100 workers: A holds 95 -> B..Z wait in queue -> p99 80ms -> 12s

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Aggregate-only metrics.
  • Averages hiding a tenant causing a tail.
  • Blaming "the network" when one tenant is the cause.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. High-cardinality metrics at 100k tenants? -> Top-K sketches or sampled per-tenant metrics; full detail for the large tenants (verify costs in the metrics system).
  2. How to alert? -> Alert on a tenant's share of a resource and on others' latency.
  3. Where is the real fix? -> Quotas, bulkheads, sharding.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE reacts to tickets. Senior instruments per tenant and attributes before an incident.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One customer's cron script every minute caused a nightly p99 spike for all.

questions.contextHtml:
At 10:02 all tenants report slow dashboards: p99 80 ms to 12 s. 500 tenants share a pool of 100 workers. Metrics excerpt:

workers_busy 100/100   queue_wait_p99 11.7s
tenant=acme  workers_held=95  job=bulk_export  started=10:00
db_cpu 35%   network normal

CPU on web nodes is low. The first suggestion is "restart everything".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restart or scale the pool; the export just takes the new workers too.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the export legitimate? Can it be paused? Does a tenant cap exist? Is this recurring?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause or throttle acme's export, cap them to a few workers, communicate with the customer.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: one tenant hogging workers (evidence in metrics); DB lock (DB CPU is 35%, a red herring); a deploy (check).
  4. How I'd verify: workers by tenant; queue wait by tenant; timeline vs deploys.
  5. Root cause: a shared pool without per-tenant limits or lanes.
  6. Fix: per-tenant concurrency cap (e.g. 10 of 100 workers), a separate lane for bulk (30 workers) and a reserved interactive lane (20), clear 429 or queued status for exports.
  7. Prevention: per-tenant dashboards, alert on one tenant over 20% of the pool.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not ban the tenant; give bulk its own capacity. Caps are product-visible; publish them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cap hurts enterprise legit usage? -> Higher quota per tier or a dedicated pool.
  • Many tenants burst together? -> Fair queueing with a per-tenant share.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single customer's migration script was the root cause of three "random" outages before per-tenant metrics existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart or scale.
  • Hire: identifies the tenant and caps it.
  • Strong hire: lanes, fair share, product-facing limits and alerts.

questions.contextHtml: A usage-based SaaS bills per API call. Today usage is counted by a usage table with UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1 per request. At 2,800 events/s, the table is a hotspot, and after a queue redelivery, customers were over-billed and an enterprise customer disputes an invoice. Finance wants hourly usage per tenant and per metric.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keep the counter and add more DB power.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How exact must billing be? Must we replay for disputes? Retention? Metrics per tenant?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Credit the disputed amount; stop in-place increments.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: non-idempotent increments and redelivery cause overcount; hot row contention.
  4. How I'd verify: compare event log counts with the counter.
  5. Root cause: counters without event ids; no durable raw log.
  6. Fix: emit usage events with event_id to a durable log; dedupe on event_id; aggregate into (tenant, metric, hour) rows: 5,000 tenants x 10 metrics x 24 = 1.2M rows/day, trivial. Keep raw events for replay in disputes.
  7. Prevention: reconcile aggregate vs raw; alerts on gaps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not bill from a mutable counter; storage for raw events is cheap compared with disputes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Late events? -> Window with a grace period, adjust next invoice.
  • Real-time quota display? -> Approximate counters in Redis; billing uses the durable one.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A replayable usage log resolved an enterprise dispute in an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: hot counter.
  • Hire: event log with dedup and aggregation.
  • Strong hire: replay for disputes, late event policy, separate quota counters.

questions.contextHtml: Revenue per tenant per month: free $0, pro $50, enterprise $10,000. Infrastructure cost per pooled tenant is $0.20/month; a dedicated database costs $300/month. Sales promised "dedicated database" to a pro customer as a perk. 20 enterprise tenants also demand it for compliance.
questions.promptHtml: What is your tenancy strategy and your answer to sales?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Dedicated DB for everyone who asks."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is isolation required by compliance or just preference? What is the churn risk? Can tiers be priced?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not agree to dedicated DBs for pro; offer a pooled tenant with higher quotas.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: margin: $300 on $50 is a loss; $300 on $10k is 3%.
  4. How I'd verify: gross margin per tier including support cost.
  5. Root cause: isolation level wasn't tied to price.
  6. Fix: hybrid: pool for free and pro; silo for enterprise above a revenue threshold; a tenant directory so promotion from pool to silo is a one-week task. Offer "dedicated" as a priced add-on.
  7. Prevention: a tier matrix (quota, isolation, SLA) and a rule that new commitments go through it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not silo everyone; 100k tenants means 100k databases.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pro tenant becomes noisy? -> Quota first, offer an upgrade.
  • Data residency requirement? -> Region-specific silo or cell.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team discovered 40 "dedicated" customers cost more than they paid.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dedicated for all.
  • Hire: hybrid by tier with math.
  • Strong hire: directory-enabled promotion, priced add-ons.

questions.promptHtml: How do you shard a multi-tenant system by tenant, and what are cells?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests routing indirection, blast radius and capacity planning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I shard by tenant using a tenant directory: a table mapping tenant to shard or cell, cached in routers. A cell is a complete, self-contained copy of the stack (app, DB, cache, queue) serving a subset of tenants, so a bad deploy or failure affects only that cell's tenants. I avoid hash-mod-N routing because adding a shard remaps everyone. Capacity planning is per cell: add a cell when average utilisation hits about 60%.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: 20 cells, each sized for 5,000 tenants and 2,000 req/s at 50% headroom. A bad deploy to cell 7 hits 5% of tenants and is rolled back by routing, not redeployed everywhere.

Client -> Router -> directory(tenant -> cell) -> Cell 7 (app, DB, cache, queue)

Moving a tenant: copy data, dual-read or short freeze, flip the directory entry, verify, delete. Cells are a heavy commitment; control plane, deployment ordering (canary cell first) and cross-cell features (global search, admin) need design.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hash-mod-N with no directory.
  • Cross-cell queries by default.
  • A single shared component (global DB) defeating blast radius.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you place a new tenant? -> Least-loaded cell or a rule by region and tier.
  2. Rebalance a hot cell? -> Move a few big tenants via the directory.
  3. Directory outage? -> Cached in routers, replicated, treat it as a tier-0 service.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: shard by tenant id hash. Senior: directory, cells, blast radius, canary cell and capacity rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cell-based rollout limited a bad migration to 5% of tenants.

questions.contextHtml: Tenant data is sharded with shard = hash(tenant_id) % 4. Four shards are at 85% disk and 70% CPU; growth is 8% monthly. Adding a fifth shard remaps about 80% of tenants. The business forbids downtime longer than a minute per tenant. Whales: 10 tenants hold 60% of the data.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a shard and rehash everyone over the weekend."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I look up tenant sizes? Cross-tenant joins? Per-tenant downtime budget? Is there a tenant directory?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Free disk (archive or compress), move the biggest tenant manually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the hash scheme blocks growth; skew from whales matters more than uniform hashing.
  4. How I'd verify: size per tenant, per-shard CPU, a histogram.
  5. Root cause: routing by a function with no indirection.
  6. Fix: introduce a tenant directory table seeded to mimic the current hash (no data moves); switch routers to read it; then move tenants one by one: bulk copy, CDC catch-up, short write freeze (under a minute), flip the entry, verify, delete. Place whales explicitly, possibly on dedicated shards.
  7. Prevention: capacity alerts at 60% disk; placement rules by load, not count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not rehash en masse; consistent hashing lessens remap but still doesn't handle whales.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Copy failed halfway? -> The directory still points to the old shard; idempotent retry.
  • Cross-tenant admin queries? -> Fan-out through a reporting store.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team introduced the directory first, and the later rebalance was routine moves rather than a project.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rehash weekend.
  • Hire: directory with per-tenant moves.
  • Strong hire: CDC catch-up, whale placement, rollback via directory.

questions.subtopic: Promoting a tenant to a silo
questions.contextHtml: Tenant "Globex" (pooled, 120 GB, 30% of the shared DB's IO) signs an enterprise deal requiring isolation and a 4-hour RPO restore of only their data. Today all tenants are in shared tables with tenant_id; no directory exists. Cutover window: max 5 minutes of read-only mode. Foreign keys cross tenant tables; some reference shared lookup tables.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: pg_dump the whole DB and filter.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Shared reference data? Time to copy 120 GB? Is tenant id on every table? Caches, search, object storage?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move Globex's heavy jobs to off-peak and apply a quota to reduce harm to others.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: tables lacking tenant_id; shared lookups; hidden state in caches and indexes.
  4. How I'd verify: schema audit for tenant columns; row counts per table for the tenant.
  5. Root cause of difficulty: no routing indirection, so the app assumes one DB.
  6. Fix: add a tenant directory and a router that selects DB per request; provision a silo with the same schema and a copy of reference data; logical replication or CDC filtered by tenant_id into the silo; when lag is seconds, set Globex read-only, drain, flip the directory (under 5 minutes), verify counts, enable writes; delete from the pool later. Also move their cache keys, search index and files.
  7. Prevention: directory from day one; all tables carry tenant_id.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not delete pool data until days later; keep rollback.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Copy lag never converges? -> Throttle writes or schedule at low traffic.
  • Schema migrations across silo and pool? -> Migration runner iterates all targets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first silo took 3 weeks; with the directory in place the second took 2 days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dump and filter.
  • Hire: CDC copy, directory flip, short read-only window.
  • Strong hire: non-DB state, rollback, migration runner.

questions.contextHtml: A schema migration rolled out to all 20 cells at once. In cell 7 an index build took an exclusive lock for 25 minutes; cell 7 (5% of tenants) was down. Other cells were fine, but the incident was only noticed after 9 minutes because dashboards were aggregated across cells and showed a 5% error rate within normal noise.
questions.promptHtml: Write the review: what went right, what went wrong, what changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Be more careful with migrations."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was there a canary cell? Per-cell alerting? Rollback plan for migrations?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route cell 7's tenants away if possible, or kill the migration; restore service.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: lock behaviour on a big table in that cell; rollout not staged; aggregate-only alerts.
  4. How I'd verify: cell 7's table size vs others; lock wait logs.
  5. Root cause: all-cell simultaneous rollout; the cell architecture's benefit (contained impact) worked, but detection and staging did not.
  6. Fix: staged rollout: canary cell first, then 10%, 50%, 100% with a bake time; per-cell SLO alerts; online migration tools (concurrent index creation, lock timeout set); automated halt on error budget burn.
  7. Prevention: migration lint (no blocking DDL without review); test on a production-sized copy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not blame the cell design; it limited the damage to 5%.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Schema change and code deploy order? -> Expand, deploy, contract.
  • Can a cell be drained? -> Yes via the directory if capacity elsewhere exists.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Per-cell dashboards cut detection from 9 minutes to 40 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "be careful".
  • Hire: staged rollout, per-cell alerts.
  • Strong hire: lock-safe DDL, auto-halt, expand-contract.

questions.contextHtml: After two noisy-neighbour incidents the CEO says "add rate limits tomorrow". The API has 500 tenants and no limits. Top tenants send 2k req/s legitimately, the median sends 5 req/s. Last quarter, 3 enterprise customers ran batch imports at 800 req/s. Sales fears breaking them. You have per-tenant metrics for 6 weeks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: A global 100 req/s cap for everyone.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which resource is scarce (workers, DB)? Which endpoints are expensive? Contractual limits? Which tenants are critical?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Protect the shared resource first with concurrency caps (e.g. max 10 workers per tenant) rather than request rates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: request counts do not reflect cost; bulk vs interactive paths differ.
  4. How I'd verify: the 6 weeks of per-tenant data: p99 usage per tenant, expensive endpoints.
  5. Root cause: no limits design, only reaction.
  6. Fix: shadow mode first: log would-be throttles for 2 weeks; set quotas per tier above observed p99 plus headroom; separate lanes for bulk (30 workers) and interactive (20 reserved); clear 429 with Retry-After; publish limits; grant temporary raises on request. Token bucket for burst plus sustained rates.
  7. Prevention: limits in the product docs; dashboards of quota use per tenant; alerts at 80%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: no global flat cap; hard limits added silently break existing customers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tenant hits limits legitimately? -> Contact, raise, or move to a bulk lane or dedicated capacity.
  • Retry storms after 429? -> Retry-After and client backoff in SDKs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Shadow mode revealed that 2 of the 3 "heavy" customers were bursts, not steady load, so a token bucket cleared them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flat global cap.
  • Hire: tiered, data-based limits with 429s.
  • Strong hire: shadow mode, concurrency caps, lanes, communication plan.
